The disc diameter of a fully grown adult Serpent star, Ophiura ophiura, typically reaches a maximum of 3.5 centimeters [Li = 3.5 centimeters], with arms extending up to 14 centimeters. This benthic brittle star inhabits the continental shelf and is frequently encountered on sandy or muddy substrates. The onset of life begins with the hatching of a small transparent egg, estimated to have a diameter of roughly 0.1 millimeters. The resulting free-swimming ophiopluteus larva emerges after a brief embryonic period; at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the larva hatches approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] after fertilisation. During this early phase, the larva is entirely yolk-dependent, relying on lecithotrophic reserves until it transitions to planktotrophic feeding. The initial wet weight of an individual at this hatching event is approximately 0.0000005236 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000005236 grams], a value consistent with the minute size of the egg from which it emerged. This extraordinarily low birth mass underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high larval mortality in the pelagic environment.

The planktonic larval phase, during which the ophiopluteus feeds on phytoplankton, lasts for a finite period before metamorphosis. Under controlled conditions maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time elapsed since birth at metamorphosis has been recorded as 17 days . At this critical transition, the bilateral larva undergoes a dramatic body plan reorganisation, during which the adult rudiment develops and the larval arms are resorbed. Upon completion of this metamorphic climax, the disc diameter at metamorphosis is exceedingly small, measuring just 0.0325 centimeters . This post-metamorphic juvenile then settles to the benthos, where it begins a benthic existence. The shift from a pelagic to a demersal lifestyle represents a significant ecological bottleneck, as the minute juvenile must immediately locate suitable microhabitats and begin exogenous feeding to sustain its rapid growth trajectory.

As juveniles grow, they gradually progress toward reproductive maturity. The disc diameter at puberty, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the achievement of sexual maturation, is reached when the central disc attains a size of 0.4 centimeters [Lp = 0.4 centimeters]. This event typically occurs a prolonged interval after settlement. In a laboratory setting at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 730 days [tp = 730 days]. This protracted developmental period, spanning roughly two years, reflects the energetic demands of building the somatic framework necessary to support eventual gamete production. At the point of sexual maturation, the ash-free dry weight at puberty is approximately 0.0016 grams . This mass is derived from the scaling relationship between disc diameter and tissue content, illustrating that even at maturity, individuals remain relatively diminutive in terms of organic matter.

Reproductively active adults are capable of sustained and prolific gamete output. The maximum reproduction rate in this species, observed under optimal thermal conditions, is remarkably high. At an experimental temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], individual females have been recorded releasing approximately 880 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 880 eggs per day]. This prodigious daily output, which represents a best estimate based on life-history scaling principles, is necessary given the extremely low survival probability of planktonic larvae in the variable coastal environment. For a fully grown adult, the ultimate ash-free dry biomass is considerable, reaching approximately 1.0681 grams . This value, representing the maximum organic mass the species can attain, reflects the culmination of years of somatic growth and tissue accumulation. The contrast between the minute mass of a hatchling and this substantial adult mass highlights the immense growth differential achieved over the species' lifetime.

The maximum lifespan of Ophiura ophiura, or the longest period an individual can persist under natural conditions, is relatively extended for a member of the family Ophiuridae, where many temperate brittle stars exhibit life cycles spanning one to three years. At a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the estimated age at natural death is approximately 1095 days [am = approximately 1095 days], representing a total life span of about three years. This longevity, which is consistent with the slow growth rates typical of cold-water brittle stars, allows for multiple reproductive seasons over an individual's lifetime. The life cycle thus encompasses a brief larval phase lasting just over two weeks, a juvenile growth period stretching nearly two years, and a mature adult stage of roughly one year during which the female can produce hundreds of thousands of eggs. This life-history strategy, balancing a high fecundity with a moderate life span, is typical of many ophiuroid species that face high larval mortality in the plankton.
